truth: A hand-held laser pointer: you sweep its bright dot across floor and walls so the cat chases it.
more: Claim 4 even sets the dot's speed, 5 to 25 feet per second: enough to exert the cat, the patent says, without discouraging the chase.
clues: It is meant for indoor pets that don't get much exercise.

A small bright spot that can never quite be caught.

prompt: Method of swinging on a swing
truth: Swinging side to side, parallel to the branch, by pulling alternately on one chain and then the other.
more: The inventor and his sister call it 'Tarzan' swinging, and a jungle yell is optional. A 2003 re-examination cancelled all four claims.
clues: Playground equipment is involved, and so is the inventor's sister.
It is about the direction you travel in.
Pull on one side, then the other.
decoys: Swinging higher by leaning back and pumping your legs hard at the top of each forward arc.
Twisting the seat round and round, then letting go so the unwinding chains spin you fast.
Standing on the seat instead of sitting, and bending your knees to push the swing along.

truth: Plastic tubes strapped over a long-eared dog's ears, holding them out sideways so they stay out of its food bowl.
more: The drawing shows a poodle. The claim requires the ear tips to end up farther apart than the width of the animal's head.
clues: It is for dogs with long, droopy ears.

decoys: Padded ear muffs for dogs that block out the noise of fireworks and thunderstorms on loud nights.
Plastic ear tags for cattle, coated with insect repellent to keep flies away all summer long.
A knitted hood for small dogs that keeps their ears warm and dry on cold winter walks.

truth: A stick: a branch-shaped dog toy for fetching and chewing, with bark texture, that floats.

truth: The comb-over: split the remaining hair into three sections and fold each over the bald patch in turn, with hair spray.
more: The patent says to grow the hair 3 to 4 inches long first. Claim 4 names the object held over each layer while styling: a hand.

Three sections, each folded over the last.

A cap with a fringe of real hair sewn inside the brim, so only the front shows.

truth: A hat with clockwork inside that lifts itself, spins and settles back on your head when you bow.

A flagpole bracket for parades that dips the flag automatically as each dignitary walks past.
A bicycle bell that plays a short, polite fanfare whenever the rider meets someone on the road.

prompt: Device for waking persons from sleep
truth: An alarm-triggered frame that drops dangling cords tipped with cork blocks onto the sleeper's face.
more: Bells fail, the inventor argued, because sleepers get used to them. Hooked to a self-lighting gas burner, it could also light the room.

truth: A clear plastic vest with tunnels, so pet hamsters or mice can crawl around your body in public view.

prompt: Apparatus for facilitating the birth of a child by centrifugal force

decoys: A rocking cradle driven by a spinning flywheel that keeps a newborn moving gently all night.

A hospital bed that slowly turns so that nurses can reach the mother from every side.

prompt: Method and means for creating anti-gravity illusion
truth: Shoes with heel slots that hook onto pegs rising from the stage, letting a dancer lean far forward without falling.

A room built on a tilt so that balls appear to roll uphill for amazed visitors.

truth: The little three-legged plastic table in a pizza box that keeps the lid from sagging onto the pizza.

decoys: A cardboard corner guard that stops parcels being crushed when they are stacked in the post.
A plastic clip that reseals a half-eaten bag of snacks so that the contents stay crisp.
A padded envelope lined with air pockets that protects fragile items sent through the mail.

Left foot, red!
decoys: Human chess: people in costume stand on a giant board and move when the players call out.

Leapfrog relay: teams vault over each other's backs in a line to reach the finish first.

truth: Cooking food with microwave radio waves from a magnetron: the method behind the microwave oven.

Coating fruit with a thin layer of wax so it stays shiny and fresh on shop shelves.
Quick-freezing fish between cold metal plates so it keeps its texture when thawed.
